newsitem.title: UK: Britain unveils plan to boost education standards.
newsitem.headline: Britain unveils plan to boost education standards.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, worried that the country's education standards are falling behind its economic rivals, unveiled plans on Monday to take greater control over schools.

Education and Employment Secretary David Blunkett published a so-called White Paper policy statement aimed at ensuring that fewer Britons grow up unable to write decent English or make elementary mathematical calculations.

"Children don't get a second chance in school. This White Paper is a vital step in our crusade to raise standards and offer opportunity to all of them," Blunkett told parliament. In the campaign for the May 1 election, Prime Minister Tony Blair repeatedly pledged that the three top priorities of his Labour government would be "education, education, and education".

He argued that literacy and numeracy standards in Britain were lagging behind those of its main economic rivals, hampering industry from entering some of the high-tech areas on which the country's commercial future would depend.

In last week's budget, finance minister Gordon Brown announced plans to increase funding to schools by some 2.3 billion pounds ($3.88 billion) to tackle building repair backlogs and provide more books and equipment.
But critics have argued the money is too little, too late and say some of it will be swallowed up by rising inflation.

The White Paper aims to raise the number of children leaving primary school at 11 who have reached the expected reading standard for that age to 80 percent by 2001 from 57 percent last year. A parallel improvement will be the target for numeracy.
The government says it will order all primary schools to devote an hour each day to the two subjects.

It says it will take powers to replace local councils in running schools which do not meet targets and warns that teachers who do not perform adequately will be subject to "speedy but fair" dismissal.
